Lessons.Title: More Standard Deviation
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: compare the spread of two contextual data sets using population standard deviation and ask for the exact missing information needed to interpret a data display. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 13, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/13/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Source roles: Building On HSS-ID.A.1; Addressing HSS-ID.A.2; Building Towards HSS-ID.A.3.

Original information-gap scenario (hypothetical, not a claim about real forests): Group A sampled four tree heights in feet 10,12,14,16; Group B measured 7,11,15,19 feet. Both means are 13 feet. Group A squared deviations from the mean are 9,1,1,9: population variance 5 and SD sqrt(5)≈2.24 ft. Group B squared deviations are 36,4,4,36: variance 20 and SD sqrt(20)≈4.47 ft. Both groups have the same center; B has greater spread.

Partner information gap: one learner holds the question 'Which group has greater variability and how much?' while the other learner holds the separate original sample values, sample units and context. The first learner requests only information needed to solve, explains why, computes independently and then exchanges the roles. The partner card's actual contents must not be invented as a real completed classroom interaction.

Interpretation: the SD of 4.47 feet describes greater spread about 13 feet than SD 2.24 feet. It is not proof every observation is 4.47 feet from the mean, nor that one group is healthier. Shifting every height up by five feet changes both means but leaves both SDs unchanged because all deviations relative to the new means are unchanged.

Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for asking relevant missing information, correct mean/SD and units, meaningful comparison acknowledging limitations, and independently justified shift-invariance claim (8 max). This info-gap reasoning and dialogue are human assessed.

Source-activity A/B review, IM Algebra 1 First Edition U01:L13: Partner info-gap: request missing context and compare two hypothetical groups by SD. Keep original first-party mathematical material and graphics; source artwork identity is NOT claimed. All physical/technology/partner work remains NOT_PERFORMED unless observed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Contextual SD
KeyConcepts.Definition: Standard deviation describes spread around a mean in the variable's original units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Interpret in the measured context without claiming each observation is exactly one SD from the mean.
KeyConcepts.Example: Group B SD≈4.47 feet signals more dispersion than Group A SD≈2.24 feet.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information gap
KeyConcepts.Definition: Ask for the sample data, units and the required statistic rather than guessing a missing value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Justify why each requested fact is needed.
KeyConcepts.Example: Raw heights and sample size allow independently computing mean and population SD.

KeyConcepts.Title: Shift invariance
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding the same constant to every observation changes mean but not SD.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Each new difference x+c-(μ+c) equals the original x−μ.
KeyConcepts.Example: Adding 5 feet to Group A changes mean 13 to 18 but leaves SD sqrt(5).

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute Group A SD
WorkedExamples.Question: For heights 10,12,14,16 feet, compute mean and population SD.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the given original data, show the computation and interpret the result in context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare Group B
WorkedExamples.Question: For 7,11,15,19 feet, compute SD and interpret.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the given original data, show the computation and interpret the result in context.
Steps: SD=sqrt(20)≈4.47 feet, twice Group A's sqrt(5).
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both means 13 feet; Group B has twice Group A's SD.
WorkedExamples.Check: sqrt(20)=2sqrt(5) and B spread is greater.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check shifting leaves SD unchanged
WorkedExamples.Question: Add five feet to every Group A height.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the given original data, show the computation and interpret the result in context.
Steps: Squared deviations still sum to 20, so variance remains 5.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Mean rises by 5 to 18 feet, population SD remains about 2.24 feet.
WorkedExamples.Check: Difference cancellation verifies invariance independent of units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reading SD as a fixed distance for every value
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: SD summarizes all squared distances and is not the distance of any given observation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Report average spread, not a universal individual distance.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing numbers without the same units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An SD in metres is not numerically comparable to feet without conversion.
A designed task is not actual classroom evidence.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the explicit hypothetical dataset and teacher observation rubric.

SummaryPoints: Interpret SD alongside the mean and measurement units.
Two groups can have equal mean but different population SDs.
Original tree-height examples have equal mean 13 feet and SDs about 2.24 versus 4.47 feet.
A constant shift changes the mean but not the SD; information-gap explanation requires teacher review.
